materials.text: Carving, engraving and fitting ivory components required practiced knowledge; one surviving part does not recover an entire hunt.

knowledge.text: Regional archaeological labels help compare artifacts; they are not one people’s unchanged political identity.

custody.text: Object attribution and regional dating are distinct, partly uncertain claims.

name: Bering Sea carvers: a tool, a design and an uncertain chronology
place: Bering Strait region; object catalogued to Alaska
geographicPrecision: Broad regional locator only. The catalogue names Alaska but no secure workshop or individual use-site; this point is not a border or excavated findspot.

interval.label: Catalogue object date, 300–500 CE; regional chronology debated
interval.note: Dates follow the current Met object record 2019.456.17. They do not define the Old Bering Sea tradition’s beginning/end. Mason and Rasic propose a later regional florescence; no new radiocarbon date for this individual object is supplied.

question: What can a beautifully made tool establish—and what must remain uncertain?
summary: A small walrus-ivory counterweight belonged to the technology of hunting at sea. Its curves and engraving connect practical work with careful visual design. Yet a museum label and a regional archaeological chronology answer different questions. We can inspect a specific surviving object without making its maker represent every Arctic community or turning a disputed chronology into a single fixed story.

sections.title: A component, not the whole hunting system
sections.text: The Met identifies this carving as a counterweight or stabilizer associated with a harpoon. Walrus ivory could be cut and engraved into a compact, shaped component. The object alone cannot show the complete shaft, line, boat, prey or sequence of a particular hunt. Identifying one tool part is a beginning for investigating work, rather than a recovered account of one hunter’s success.

citations.locator: Description: counterweight/stabilizer, walrus ivory and harpoon use

sections.title: Design takes skill; meaning takes evidence
sections.text: Follow the curving lines across the surface. The catalogue cautiously suggests animal features at the top and outer edges. That suggestion is not a certain identification of every form or a transcription of the carver’s beliefs. Shape and ornament both involved decisions, but an attractive object does not establish equal wealth or tell us who was entitled to make, own or interpret it.

citations.locator: Description: engraved curvilinear designs and possible animal features

sections.title: Two kinds of date should not be collapsed
sections.text: The museum gives this object 300–500 CE. In the research abstract published by NPS, Mason and Rasic discuss corrections for marine carbon and propose an Old Bering Sea florescence of 650–1250, with earlier related contexts. These are different evidential claims: an object catalogue attribution and a revision of regional dating. This atlas retains both with their scopes. It neither silently redates the carving nor calls the whole question settled.

citations.locator: Abstract, chronology revision and marine-carbon correction

sections.title: A region of relationships, not one frozen people
sections.text: The same research investigates walrus haul-out sites, seafaring technology, movement and relationships between communities. NPS’s Birnirk account explains how archaeologists compare tool styles at a type-site. Such labels organize material evidence; they are not the names of one timeless Arctic state. This investigation does not use a carved tool to invent a direct genealogy for every later Inuit, Iñupiat or Yupik community.

citations.locator: Walrus sites, migration and social/technological explanations

sections.title: Learning is work between people
sections.text: Kawerak’s public report brings a different kind of evidence: artists’ accounts from interviews and focus groups in 2019. Participants describe learning with relatives and mentors, and sharing, giving or buying materials. These accounts make practice and relationships part of the explanation of skilled work. They concern living artists; they do not identify the ancient carver or settle the catalogue date.

claims.text: The Met dates this counterweight 300–500 CE, while Mason/Rasic’s later regional chronology concerns a different level of evidence; the latter does not individually redetermine this carving’s date.

deeperReading.title: Ask what was dated
deeperReading.text: A catalogue range groups a particular object by the museum’s attribution. A regional chronology compares evidence from multiple contexts. Mason and Rasic’s abstract says that marine-carbon corrections change the regional dating argument; reading that abstract does not reproduce their full tables or calibration work. The proposed later florescence therefore stays visible beside the museum’s 300–500 range. It is not applied as an unreported new measurement of this carving. The gift credit adds a third kind of date: 2019 records a modern museum acquisition, not manufacture or the beginning of the object’s custody history.

deeperReading.title: A public community account has its own scope
deeperReading.text: Kawerak commissioned research with artists from different communities, including Iñupiaq, Central Yup’ik and St. Lawrence Island Yupik participants. Its selected accounts describe learning and access to materials. The report is a source for those participants’ experiences, not a census or permission to speak for everyone. It supplies neither a translation of the ancient engravings nor a demonstrated transmission from this individual object to one modern artist. The report’s exact publication date remains unestablished; its 2019 interviews are explicitly dated.

evidenceReading.title: Separate a visible detail, a dating proposal and an artist account
evidenceReading.introduction: The following are editorial paraphrases. Each source answers a different question; none supplies the missing voice of this object’s maker.

items.label: A shaped and engraved component
items.text: The photographs show curved arms and surface lines. The Met identifies walrus ivory and interprets the object as a harpoon counterweight or stabilizer, with possible animal features.
items.interpretation: Description and functional interpretation can support an account of skill without recovering a whole hunt, certain meaning for every form, or a named owner. Display supports visible in the photograph are not ancient tool parts.

citations.locator: Actual three views and visible description

items.label: Two dates with different subjects
items.text: The catalogue dates this carving 300–500 CE. Mason and Rasic propose a regional Old Bering Sea florescence of 650–1250 after marine-carbon corrections.
items.interpretation: The regional proposal should prompt a question about chronology, not an automatic replacement of the individual catalogue date. No new assay for accession 2019.456.17 was established in this consultation.

items.label: Learning and materials in a living community account
items.text: Kawerak’s report describes participants learning with relatives and mentors and exchanging materials. Its methods place the interviews and focus groups in 2019.
items.interpretation: These are attributed modern experiences, not an ancient biography, a universal community statement or approval to reproduce every design. Anonymous speakers remain anonymous.

familyActivity.title: Three evidence cards
steps: Use the full-object and alternate views. Point to a carved curve and a surface line. Keep the pale display rod and metal supports separate from the ivory component.

Read this capsule: the Met catalogues the object to 300–500 CE. A regional research abstract proposes an Old Bering Sea florescence of 650–1250. A Kawerak report describes artists learning with relatives and mentors in interviews and focus groups held in 2019.

Make three cards headed “object catalogue,” “regional dating proposal” and “modern artist account.” Put each date and one supported statement on the correct card. Which card can identify this ancient maker?
familyActivity.explanation: The catalogue card records 300–500 and the identified tool component. The regional card records the proposed 650–1250 range. The artist-account card records the 2019 interviews and learning relationships. None names this carving’s maker. The three sources can inform one investigation while answering different questions.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author checking; not independent historian or community approval
review.scope: A registry KEEP case: the existing four main sections are retained and one bounded community-source section is added, with deeper reading, evidence interpretation, a supplied family capsule and a separately qualified reference. The complete original interval, identity, claims, dimension texts, coordinates, object order, media metadata and image bytes remain protected.
limitations: The object’s maker, secure excavated findspot, exact original use, full early custody and photographic exposure date remain unestablished. Possible animal features and tool function remain catalogue interpretations; no individual radiocarbon redating was established.

Regional chronology is reported at abstract level. The publisher full text returned 403 and was not retried or bypassed; complete tables, calibration models, original assays and supplements were not read. Birnirk’s explicit NPS date range is attributed, not a resolved universal chronology.

The Kawerak report’s publication date is unknown here; its 2019 interview date is known. Selected pages, anonymous participant accounts and a non-census sample do not establish a universal voice, direct lineage from this carving, or permission to reproduce a community design.

No new media, tracing, annotation, historical route, surveyed point or site-access instruction is supplied. Report-photo consent for its own publication is not treated as a new reuse licence. The existing Met image rights and all three view files remain unchanged.
